senses: The act of disbanding
An emergent tropical rainforest tree, Koompassia excelsa, family Fabaceae, of Southeast Asia.
examples: The honey-bee of Borneo very generally hangs its combs under the branches of the Tappan, a tree which towers above all others in the forest, and whose smooth cylindrical trunk often rises a hundred feet without a branch.

senses: The second part of a piano duet for four hands.
The course that follows the antipasto and primo courses in a full course Italian meal; the meat or fish course.
A second-generation migrant to Switzerland; The child of an immigrant to Switzerland.
examples: The writing carefully develops equality in the pupil's hands, as well as fostering a keen sense of hearing through interaction with the more complex writing in the secondo part.
Whereas the first part of the dance is light and vivacious, the mood now turns more pompous, with heavy off-beats in the secondo right hand.
In the tenor, the first p. 30 has the secondo choro (C2) and the second p. 30 has the primo choro (C4) for both.

senses: A Japanese fish-shaped cake with various fillings.
ety: From Japanese たい焼き, literally "baked sea bream".
examples: Taiyakis are made right here, all during the day, and are especially yummy when they when they are immediately made and hot off the grill. They are also great as a mid-morning or afternoon snack.
A woman fed a brood of lettuce hens taiyakis.
Another stall there, Mama, does croissant taiyakis, fish-shaped pastries with a choice of custardy fillings.

senses: A charitable house to receive and care for sick people, later distinguished from a hospital as being especially for those of a low class or meagre financial means.
ety: From Middle English spitel, an aphetic form, from Medieval Latin hospitāle.

senses: The pileus of certain fungi.
ety: Borrowed from Latin umbella (“umbrella”). Compare umbrella, composed of the same etymological elements but formed independently.

senses: A short concerto.
The group of solo instruments in a concerto grosso.
A section in a concerto grosso played by three instruments.
ety: Borrowed from Italian concertino, from concerto + -ino (diminutive suffix).

senses: A person who settles property on express trust for the benefit of beneficiaries.
A combination of a cardigan and a jumper, usually knitted in wool or cashmere.
A pair of cars or locomotives that are permanently coupled and treated as a single unit.
examples: I need these people, the Sergeant, and Mr. Tighe the shopman in the village, even Miss Broaders, she of the pink twinsets and tight mouth, who presides over the post office.
She had been out all day campaigning and looked stiffly immaculate as ever in a royal blue twinset — except for her nose, which was twitching uncontrollably in disgust.
Shand's father had missed the whole thing — getting fou in the pub, more than likely—but his mum had been there, in her best green twinset, her court shoes polished to a shine as high as Shand's.

senses: Larger than grande, usually 20 ounces (~ 0.6 l).
Dewormer, medicine used in deworming an animal.
Vermicide, any substance used to kill worms.
examples: Dung beetles dived into delicious organic cowpats left by longhorn cattle that hadn’t been fed wormers and parasiticides
If demand for the herbs is high we can add more wormers to the lobby and basement.

senses: One who finds a way: either a physical route or a means to achieve something.
Lactobacillus acidophilus, one of the bacteria commonly used in fermenting yogurt
A person, especially a male one, who reports the weather conditions or forecasts.
The treatment of people in a fatherly manner, especially by caring for them and sometimes being stern with them.
The guiding of people in a manner that limits their autonomy in the name of their own well-being.
Used to describe someone or something that shows commitment; committed, attractive, cool.
ety: From for + the. Popularized by the Canadian sitcom Letterkenny.

senses: A footpath near a road.
ety: From Middle English side-way, side-wei, equivalent to side + way.

senses: A traditional Jewish prayer shawl with tassels which covers the chest and upper part of the back.
Any of several varieties of aromatic black tea from China.
ety: Borrowed from Cantonese 小種 /小种 (siu² zung², “subvariety”). See also Hokkien 小種茶 /小种茶 (sió-chióng-tê).

senses: A comb, required to be worn at all times by Sikhs, one of the five Ks.
An expression of praise to God, especially a short hymn sung as part of a Christian worship service.
ety: From Medieval Latin doxologia, from Ancient Greek δοξολογία (doxología, “a praising”), from δοξολόγος (doxológos, “giving or uttering praise”), from δόξα (dóxa, “glory, honor, repute”), from δοκέω (dokéō, “to think, expect”).

senses: A person who is granted bail.
examples: If the bailee fails to appear at trial, he or she forfeits the full bond amount and must still stand trial — if he or she is ever located.

senses: Homosexual, gay or lesbian, having a sexual or romantic preference for persons of one's own gender; used to emphasize love over sex.
examples: It seems that many homophile Bostonians don't patronize Provincetown for various reasons. Wake-up you homophile brothers and sisters. You have a great resort in your own backyard.

senses: Requiring or showing effort.
examples: It is obvious, therefore, that syntopical reading is the most active and effortful kind of reading.

senses: A policy of formally complying with efforts to achieve a goal by making small, token gestures; especially to hire a minimal number of ethnically diverse or disadvantaged people.
examples: We know the prime minister regards environmental matters as mere tokenism. But we at least expected his ritual once-a-year speech on the issue.

Contemporary museums, they need to stop tokenism. Collect an Iranian artist here, a South African artist there or whatever. They need to really begin to try to properly take on … what is contemporary culture today?
This has to be meaningful contribution and participation – tokenism will only come to bite us in the future.

senses: A biobank where cryogenically preserved material is stored.
examples: In the early 1970s, the first cryobanks, largely run by men, opened in the United States, offering frozen sperm from anonymous donors (often college students), mostly to infertile couples.

senses: Having a taste of hops; heavily flavoured with hops.
A large black gibbon, Symphalangus syndactylus, from Sumatra.
A room used as a barrier between indoors and outdoors.
examples: We made sure to hang our wet clothes on the hook in the mudroom when we came in from the snow.

senses: Of feathers, hair, etc.: crisped or curled; crinkled, frizzed; also, of a person's head, etc.: covered with curled hair, or something similar to that.
examples: Who there frequents at these unmodish hours, / But ancient matrons with their frizzled towers, / And grey religious maids?

senses: An aubergine or eggplant.
ety: Borrowed from Portuguese beringela, from Old Galician-Portuguese berengenha, borrowed from Arabic بَاذِنْجَان (bāḏinjān), borrowed from Classical Persian بَاذِنْگَان (bāzingān), borrowed from Sanskrit वातिङ्गण (vātiṅgaṇa), from Proto-Dravidian *waẓVtV. Doublet of aubergine, malidzano, and melongene.

senses: An administrator on a wiki.
A kind of anyon with statistical properties between those of fermions and bosons.
Often preceded by a descriptive word: one who modifies a mass-manufactured object, especially computer hardware or software, or a motor vehicle.
ety: From mod (“to modify (an object) from its original condition”) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns).

senses: An unlined cotton summer kimono worn by both men and women.
ety: From Japanese 浴衣(ゆかた) (yukata), originally short for 湯帷子(ゆかたびら) (yukatabira, “kimono worn during or after bathing”).
examples: When made of lightweight cotton, the unlined and partially lined kimono become yukata. Yukata, however, do not have flutter sleeves, as they are considered too dressy for this informal kimono.
Most Japanese now wear yukata as summer kimono that are cool and comfortable.

senses: A hospital or school for orphans.
Synonym of music school.
ety: Borrowed from Italian conservatorio, from the musical education provided there for orphans, from Medieval Latin conservatorium, from conservatus (“conserved, preserved”) + -orium (“-ory”).

senses: A mixture of plaster of Paris and glue used to prepare a surface for painting.
A work of art done in gesso.
ety: Borrowed from Italian gesso. Doublet of gypsum. Compare Portuguese gesso (“gypsum; plaster, cast”) and Spanish yeso (“gypsum; plaster, cast”).

senses: Characterized by gales of wind.
That cannot be picked.
The horizontal portion of the face that includes the eyes.
Line of sight.
The direction in which an actor or presenter is looking.
examples: They realise that trajectories, space expansion and crushing are different with different lenses, whether wide angle or telephoto, and that actors' eyelines will be altered.
